utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Ms. Gustafson, I was informed that you'd like to make a correction to the transcript of yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yesterday, I was informed by Mr. Misetic that I referred to a document that formed part of 65 ter number 1571. Incorrectly, I stated that it was a report of a disciplinary measure to General Gotovina, and Mr. Misetic was correct. It's, in fact, a report to the legal department of the Split Military District, and that was at transcript page 10856, line 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is about tab 12, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for this correction. Are you ready to continue your examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Ms. Botteri, I'd like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you gave yesterday at the beginning of your testimony. Ms. Gustafson, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and just before commencing, I'd like to inform the Court that I may need more time that was originally planned for this witness. It was originally scheduled for two and a half hours, and if could I have to the end of the second session this morning, I would endeavour to finish sooner, of course, but I may need to the end of the second session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll see how the testimony develops.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: One or matter before I begin, Your Honour. Yesterday, I neglected to tender the documents that I referred to, which was the Code of Military Discipline, 65 ter number 1834; and the disciplinary reports that I referred to, the two cases of burning, 65 ter number 6012 and the five cases involving theft, and these are 65 ter numbers 6013, 157, and 6031, if I could have exhibit numbers for those, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, first for the Code, 1834.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 1834 becomes Exhibit number P1007; 65 ter 6012 becomes Exhibit number P1008; 65 ter number 6013 becomes Exhibit number P1009; 65 ter 1571 becomes Exhibit number P1010; 65 ter number 6031 becomes Exhibit number P1011.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections; therefore, P1007 up to and including P1011 are admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I could have 65 ter 6018, this is the second shorter chart that I distributed yesterday, titled "Disciplinary actions taken by Ante Gotovina, in August and September 1995." If the witness could be given a hard copy of the documents referred to in this chart.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, this is a bundle of documents that's the same as the ones you were given a few days ago, with the addition of an Index at the front, dealing with disciplinary actions taken by General Gotovina in August and September, 1995. Do you recall being given the same bundle of documents a few days ago?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And were these -- are these documents, documents would you have seen at the time in August or September 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And is this group of documents, the actions that they reflect, are those actions consistent with your recollection of the disciplinary actions taken by General Gotovina at that time, in August and September of 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. However, I am not certain of the number of real instance and what I'm seeing or being shown here.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If I could have an exhibit number for the chart, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number P1012.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since I hear of no objections, P1012 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm going only to direct you, this morning, to one group of documents in the chart, and those are the documents behind tab number 9 and that's entry number nine in the chart.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: These documents are in 65 ter 5991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, purely as a technical matter, I don't think leave had been granted for the exhibit that was just admitted into evidence to be added to the 65 ter list, so I don't know if procedurally you wish to fulfil that formality as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, was that included in tendering that you also sought leave to have if added to the 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I neglected to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I understand the absence of any objections to include adding the document to the 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the decision stands as it was and is completed with a formal leave being granted for it to be admitted to the 65 ter list before it was admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, if you could look at the first page in this bundle, which should be the same document that's on the screen in front of you, you'll see that this is an order dated 29 August 1995 by General Gotovina, ordering the formation of a commission, and that included the department commander of the 4th Guards Brigade, as well as the Deputy Commander of the 72 Military Police Battalion, and included three members of your command: Yourself; Major Milas, assistant commander for security an information service; and Colonel Zelic, who you have said in your statement was the assistant commander for political activity and information. And according to this order, the commission was tasked with identifying the name and the unit of each perpetrator of a number of HV soldiers who had taken -- illegally taken over some flats in Split; and the commission was also ordered to, in collaboration with the 72 Military Police Battalion, file criminal reports with the military prosecutor against the perpetrators and their superiors, and to report to General Gotovina on the matter within seven days with a copy of the military disciplinary records and criminal reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next document, which should be page 4 in B/C/S and page 3 in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is a document dated 8th September 1995, and it's a report from General Gotovina to General Cervenko of the Main Staff. You can see that under point 2, General Gotovina reports that the owner of each flat and the name of each -- of the perpetrator for each flat has been identified. Under point 4, he describes the current situation, how many perpetrators have moved out, how many have promised to move out, and how many have refused to move out. At point 5, he describes -- describes what took place. At point 6, discusses the responsibility of superior officers. Under point 7, he stats that the commander of the 4th Guards Brigade would implement disciplinary measures, and the 72 Military Police Battalion will file criminal reports against perpetrators who do not move out. At this stage, I'd just like to ask you: It appears from this report from General Gotovina that the commission was successful in establishing the facts and identifying the perpetrators in relation to this incident. Would you agree with that, as a member of this commission? Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, on this point, in your -- the statement you gave to the Defence at paragraph 5, you noted that it was not a regular practice to initiate disciplinary inquiries against unknown offenders. And in this case, as you have seen, the commission was tasked with identifying the perpetrators of -- in this incident. My question is: Do you know why in this particular case a disciplinary inquiry was initiated in the case of unknown perpetrators when, as you've said, it was not common practice within the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe since her Defence statement is in evidence and the question is "Why," I believe her attention then should be drawn to what is already in evidence; and to that extent, the objection formally, then, should be asked and answered. But she lays that out in her answer to question 18 which begins on page 8 of the Defence statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the question was a more specific one which was, in light of the general proposition that she made in her Defence statement, why it was that an exception to the general practice was made, and that matter is not discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Then the objection, Your Honour, is that it calls for speculation because the answer to the question is that this was formed because a superior officer to General Gotovina ordered that such a commission be formed. So, that it extent, it calls for knowing why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even if we know who ordered it and whether it was ordered, sometimes people have knowledge of why such an order was issued. So the witness may answer the question. Perhaps you repeat it, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, the question was: Why was an exception to the general rule that disciplinary inquiries were not formed to investigate matters of unknown perpetrators in this particular case?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by what I said before, that disciplinary action was not taken against unknown perpetrators. In this particular case, the -- the first phase of this inquiry is not of military disciplinary character. The commission that was formed is a war-time commission that was entrusted the investigation of this incident, in order to obtain or discover the names of perpetrators. We had some information at our disposal because if you take a look at this entire case file, you will see that we had some indicia which could point to the names of the perpetrators; in other words, only after this commission actually learned the names of the perpetrators and their action did we actually initiate the disciplinary procedure. So these are two completely different matters. The commission that was appointed discovered the perpetrators, so once that was done, there was no longer -- it was no longer possible to speak of unknown perpetrators. At the point when a criminal complaint is filed, the perpetrators are familiar because this commission actually did its job as it should have.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, I don't think anyone's disputing that an individual disciplinary measure can't be taken against an unknown perpetrator for the very fact that the perpetrator is unknown, but your statement dealt with disciplinary inquiries, and you've said that the first phase of this inquiry was not of a military a military disciplinary character. But in paragraph 1 of the order, General Gotovina tasks the commission to establish the facts and propose measures to evict members of the HV who forcibly moved in, and to propose measures to discipline the perpetrators. Are you disputing that this was an order to undertake, at least in part, a disciplinary inquiry?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not an inquiry.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: What would you call it then?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conduct of an investigation for which we had certain indicia which could have help discover the perpetrators, precisely because in each particular case, we sought to actually carry out whatever we were supposed to, under the laws and regulation.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can ascertain here that this -- these were two different matters here. I still stand by what I said earlier, that inquiries were not undertaken against unknown perpetrators; and in this particular case, that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move on. Just before I do, I'd like it confirm the class number at the top of page 1, the page you have before you, 114-03/95-01/02. That class number refers to disciplinary matters. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand your question. Which numbers are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm referring to class number at the top of the first page. I believe it's the page you have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 1 in e-court, it should be there as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Do you see the class number 114-03 --

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The class reference number, right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That class number refers to disciplinary category?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, could I seek a clarification of your answer. This order states that the commission is charged with tasks, among them, the task to propose disciplinary measures for the perpetrators responsible. Doesn't this qualify the order as at least, in part, dealing with an investigation, among other matters, for the purposes of collecting facts or establishing facts for the purpose of taking disciplinary measures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, well, that's what I said, that this commission dealt with conducting inquiries in order to establish certain facts, identify perpetrators, so that that could serve as a basis for instituting liability proceedings, either in disciplinary court or in a criminal court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could move to page 7 in the English and page 8 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, this should be the third document in the bundle. It's dated the 8th of September, 1995, as well, and it's an order from General Gotovina to the command of the 4th Guards Brigade and the commander of the 72nd Military Police Battalion. He -- in this order, he orders the 4th Guards Brigade commanding officer and the 72nd Military Police Battalion commanding officer to take steps -- sorry, the 4th Guards Brigade commanding officer to impose disciplinary measures and the 72nd Military Police Battalion commanding officer to file criminal charges against the perpetrators who do not move out of the flats immediately after returning from the field. You've discussed this order in your Defence statement at paragraph 18, and you said: "Based on the order by General Cervenko, the Split Military District commander ordered the military police here two things: Participation in solving the situation regarding the illegal entry and securing the work of the commission. The Split Military commander was authorised to order both, pursuant to Article 9 of the rules governing the structure an operation of the military police because it was part of their daily police work. "It is a matter of police activity where the commander is, in fact, providing the police with information that they should act in a manner already prescribed by the rules on their operation. Besides, what is also important is that in this case, General Gotovina acted entirely according to the rules and guidelines given to him by the chief of the Main Staff." I'd just like to clarify this part of your answer in your Defence statement here, because you referred to Article 9 of the military police rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this is in evidence as P880.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That rule in the relevant states: "While performing their regular military police tasks, military police units are subordinate to the commander of the Military District in the military police units' areas of operations." As you can see, and as I'm sure you know, Article 9 refers to the subordination of the military police to the Military District commander for certain tasks and does not mention the Main Staff. So, when you said that General Cervenko's guidelines to Gotovina in relation to this incident were also important, my question is: From a strictly legal perspective, did General Cervenko's guidelines have anything to do with General Gotovina's legal authority to give these orders to the military police in relation to this incident?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be grateful if you would clarify the question. Legal authority in what sense?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, you said in your statement that General Gotovina was authorised to issue this order to the military police because it was part of their daily police work, and you referred to Article 9 of the rules for the military police. My question to you is: Did General Gotovina have this authority pursuant to Article 9 to issue the orders that you see in this documents irrespective of the fact that he was following General Cervenko's guidelines?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In keeping with the provisions of Article 9 of the rules on the operation of military police, General Gotovina had powers only within the framework of the provisions of Article 9, but I said in my statement that the fact should not be neglected that General Gotovina also received a similar order from his own direct superior. It's not that he was acting unlawfully just because he received the order from his direct superior.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So, if I understand you correctly, General Gotovina's authority to take these measures stemmed from Article 9. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know personally how this matter was resolved, whether any measures were taken against these perpetrators or whether they agreed to move out of the apartments; or do you know, generally speaking, what happened?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall the details, but from what I see in the documents and knowing how things were done at that time, I'm sure that everything was done as described in the file itself. That means that some of them who had moved in illegally moved out, and all the measures that were envisaged were, indeed, taken: Disciplinary proceedings but also criminal proceedings, as indicated in the file. So it is not based on my recollection. It's based on my general knowledge and observations, because I lived there at the time, and I`m sure that this was, indeed, implemented as stated in the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And one last question on these documents. In your Defence statement, you said that you believed that these housing cooperatives had turned to the chief of the Main Staff with the hope that the issue would be resolved more efficiently given that the court procedure in these cases was very slowly. Based on your involvement with the commission and your review of these documents, would you say that the problem was, indeed, resolved efficiently through the mechanisms implemented by the chief of the Main Staff and by General Gotovina in this case?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still don't understand your question. I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters would be grateful if extra microphones could be switched off.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: My question is: Based on your involvement in the commission and your review of these documents, would you say that this was an efficient resolution to the problem of HV soldiers illegally occupying flats?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was certainly more efficient than if things had taken the regular court channels, because court proceedings are very slow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I seek one clarification of one of the previous answers. Ms. Botteri, you said, when asked about what was the follow-up, what happened, you said: "Some of them who had moved in illegally moved out, and all the measures that were envisaged were, indeed, taken: Disciplinary proceedings but also criminal proceedings, as indicated in the file." Then you say: "So it is not based on my recollection. It's based on ..." There the transcript is not perfectly clear. You said you lived there at the time. Could you tell us where it appears in the documentation that criminal prosecution was instituted and how, by living there, you could know that people were prosecuted or disciplined.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know because both as a lawyer and a citizen, I was familiar with the legal system and how it operated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, let's make a clear distinction between how a system is supposed to operate and how it, in fact, operates. So what I'd like to know, if you say, I can tell you that these people were prosecuted or disciplined, I'm not interested in knowing how the system provided for the possibility and perhaps even the duty to discipline or to prosecute people, but I'm interested in what actually happened and how you would know that these persons were actually prosecuted. You said it is not from your memory but it is because you lived there and because you -- on the basis of the documentation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Criminal responsibility was established in legal proceedings before regular courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I stop you there. I do understand that criminal responsibility is established in a court. What I'd like it know, in what court, against these people, criminal responsibility was established or perhaps they were acquitted. I don't want a description of the system. I want a description of what happened in that system, in relation to these persons, in relation to these acts. And if you don't know, fine, then tell us; if you do know, tell us what you know, and not about what was supposed to happen in a system.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we're talking about military disciplinary liability, all offenders were supposed to be disciplined by their military superiors. If we're talking about criminal responsibility, then it was the military police that filed criminal reports --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- or should have filed criminal reports to the state prosecutor. Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, I think you are intelligent enough to know that the distinction between what should happen and what happens, as a trained lawyer. For example, I read, on page 7, that it was ordered that the 72nd Military Police Battalion commanding officer shall file criminal charges through his specialist staff to the military prosecutor's office in Split. What I want to know is whether what was ordered, whether you have any knowledge on whether that was done, yes or no. It seems a rather simple question. I know who should have done it, but what I would like to know is whether it was done, yes or no, if you know. If you don't know, tell us; if do you know, fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot have knowledge about this, whether it was really down, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I had no control over the functioning of the legal system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can tell you that I sometime have knowledge of matters which are not within my control. So for the answer "I can't have any knowledge," what I am interested in is to know whether you have knowledge. Whether you could have had knowledge is a different question, whether you were in control is a different question. It's just do you know or do you not know. I take from your answer that you just don't know whether it happened or not, that you expect it to have happened, because of the system, but that have you no actual knowledge of it. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, do you recall any other similar commissions or inquiries set up in August or September of 1995 to investigate any other incidents of alleged misconduct by HV members?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot remember specific cases. It was a really long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: But you remember this case. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I see a specific case file, it refreshes my memory; but, generally speaking, I cannot remember cases individual cases, which means that if I saw perhaps some more case files, I would recall them eventually. But just like this, when you ask me, I don't. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can I seek further clarification of this answer. Ms. Botteri, you say: "I cannot remember individual cases." Can you positively confirm that there were other cases where such a commission was established, so even if you don't remember what it was all about, but that you know that there have been orders establishing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you give us an indication about the number of times such a commission was established. Was it one other commission, five other commissions, 20? Could you give us an indication? I'm not asking for a precise number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really cannot remember the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I'm asking an indication of the number. Could that have been one other commission, or quite a number, 10, 20? You have no recollection as approximately how often you saw a situation where such a commission was established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My estimate is that there was a large number of such commissions, and the reason I cannot give you even a rough number, like 50, 100, or 1.000, is that I was not in a position to learn about it every time such a commission was formed and because I didn't always have access to such information. Maybe there had been many commissions at lower levels, not only at the level of the command where I worked. Nevertheless, within the whole system, these other commissions dealt with enforcing military discipline in the whole Military District.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you said that your estimate was that it was a large number. Could you give us an estimate on the level of which you had knowledge, because, at the same time, you say large number, but I might have not known about them. Now, on what is your estimate based on other than commissions you may not have been informed about, because that comes down to speculation, rather than to an estimate. You were referring to the lower levels. Now, at the level of the command you worked in - you made that distinction - could you give us an indication on how many commissions were established on that level, where, apparently, you had knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you positively confirm that at that command level there were more commissions established than the one we just talked about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us an approximate indication of how many of the commissions were established at that level, 1, 5, 20, whatever it is? Of course, I should add perhaps 1, approximately 5, approximately 10, 100. Could you tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's difficult for me to recall specific numbers. I would appreciate it if you could clarify whether you are really asking me about military disciplinary commissions or perhaps commissions that had other tasks from other sectors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When I'm talking about similar commissions, I'm talking about a commission like this one, who was tasked with an inquiry, perhaps among other matters, but also for the purpose of establishing facts to see whether any disciplinary measures should be taken or whether any criminal prosecutions should be undertaken.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that makes it easier to answer, perhaps, because my knowledge, or rather, conclusions about the number of such commissions comes -- come from the fact that there was a large number of military disciplinary proceedings at the time. So, as far as I can judge, there could have been even 500 or a thousand, not commissions but proceedings, cases. But sometimes these cases may have been handled by individuals, not only commissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking about commissions, that's clear, isn't it? I'm talking about the establishment of such commissions. What your are doing is making is a big circle and my question and then finally say, well, there were a lot of disciplinary proceedings so there could have been. Do you have any knowledge? I want to know not whether you can draw any conclusions, but whether have you any knowledge of similar commissions being established at your command level. If you don't have knowledge, tell us; if you have, tell us what you know about approximate numbers, because that's what I asked for.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot give you a precise answer, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can't give me a precise answer on an approximate number of such commissions being established at your command level. Is that correctly understood? I'm not asking for a precise number; I'm asking for an approximate number. If you don't know, please tell us, but you tell us you can't give us a precise answer, which suggests that you could give us an unprecise answer. If that is the case, tell what you say your unprecise answer is; if not, tell us that you can't answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot answer your question. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I could tender those documents into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There a lot of documents I don't have any objection, but I think we have gone through quite a few.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are three documents --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Forming a case file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I see is that, on e-court, I have nine pages in total, consisting of three documents; is that correct? I think my last quote was from the semi-last document. They're uploaded under what 65 ter number, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, 5991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it's the case file. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number Exhibit number P1013.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1013 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Botteri, a few moments ago, we were talking about the military police and the role of the military police in the Split Military District structure. You've given some information about that in your various statements. In the first statement, 2004, you said: "For their regular daily police work, the military police would be under the command of General Gotovina whilst they were working in the Military District Split." In your second statement, you said: "In operational terms, the 72nd Military Police Battalion was subordinated to the Split Military District, and I think that the commander of the Split Military District was authorised to issue orders from within their scope of activity, in accordance with the standard operating procedures of military police." And in your statement to the Defence of a few days ago, you said: "In practice, the Split Military District commander could have issued orders for the so-called daily police work. This entails work planned in securing and escorting a vehicle column, et cetera; however, with basic military police tasks, such as preventing criminal offences and detecting perpetrators of the same, an order issued by the Split Military District commander in these case would say not be relevant. "The prevention of committing criminal offences and protecting perpetrators, criminal processing of objects, conducting criminal investigative actions had to be done by the military police in accordance with their legal responsibility and in accordance with a warrant by the military prosecutor, i.e., the investigating judge." Now, I just want it clarify those various answers. At the stage before there's any form investigation, before there's the involvement of the prosecutor or an investigating judge, I'm talking here about basic military police tasks, like patrolling, setting up check-points, stopping members of the army who are caught committing crime, reporting those crimes, filing criminal reports in relation to such perpetrators, those kind of basic tasks. Those tasks didn't require a warrant by the military prosecutor or an investigating judge. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I object to the form of the question, Your Honour. The characterisation of certain aspects as basic tasks may be something this disputed by the parties, so it is leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's then refrain from the basic tasks but those tasks that you described, Ms. Gustafson, is that what you'd like the witness to focus her answer on?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, those tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So whether those tasks ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first statement that I gave to the Prosecutor, yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: My question was: Is a warrant from an investigating judge or a prosecutor required in order for the military police to conduct those tasks.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in every case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, could you mention for us any case in which you would need the warrant from an investigating judge or a prosecutor when you are patrolling, setting up check-points or stopping members of the army who are caught committing a crime, and then reporting those crimes and filing criminal reports in relations to them. Could you give us an example of where you would, to perform those tasks, where you would need a warrant by a prosecutor or an investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not participate in this work. This had to do with the cooperation between the court and the police. So, the police, in keeping with their rules of service of the military police, carried out their duties. They submitted reports, criminal reports, to the state prosecutor, and that is how the police and the state prosecutor worked together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Your answer was, to the question of Ms. Gustafson, when she asked you whether a warrant of an investigating judge or a prosecutor was required to conduct those tasks, you said: "No, not in every case," which suggests that you had cases on your mind, whether such a warrant would be needed. I'm asking you whether you could give us an example of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't give you an example because I did not take part in this portion of the work. I did not work for the court or the military police. But the cooperation between the military police and the state prosecutor was twofold. The military police, in the course of their duties, if they learned of a criminal offence and submitted a criminal report to the state prosecutor, the state prosecutor could then take some actions in order to resolve -- to solve the case, or ask the police to supplement the case with some additional investigative actions. My answer, as I gave it, was in this context; however, I did not work either for a court or the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what you're saying --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was irrelevant for my job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I understand your answer to be the following: These tasks were performed without such a warrant, but once it had been reported that there was a possibility that for follow-up investigations, that a prosecutor, for example, would give further instructions. Is that understood well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would not call it "instructions," but, rather, a request for additional actions, investigative actions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking you because you're making the distinction between some cases where there were such warrants and others. You say not in all cases. So I'm trying to understand what you fully meant, but it is clear to me now. Please proceed, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, in relation to these tasks where there was no involvement from the prosecutor or the investigating judge, for these tasks, would an order from General Gotovina be relevant to these tasks? For example, an order from General Gotovina to the military police to set up a check-point in a certain location, would that be a relevant order?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise for the interruption, but a -- relevant to what?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness herself used the word relevant, Mr. Misetic. So, if you say this is irrelevant if he gave such an order, specifically in relation to the authority of others, if you look at it in the context of the answer of the witness, I think that the question is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Okay. Well, I just don't understand what a check-point has to do with an investigating judge. I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. That's exactly what Ms. Gustafson is asking about. You understand her perfectly well, and it's a follow-up to one of the answers given by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can we cite that, then, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we have to find it. But just from my memory, she said that such an order would not be relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It's from the Defence statement, Your Honour, the answer to question 16 in the Defence witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that be --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It says: "Basic military police tasks such as preventing criminal offences and detecting perpetrators, an order issued by the Split Military District commander in these case would say not be relevant."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct. So what is check-point? That's my point --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Then it goes on to talk about actions requiring a warrant. I think the question is perfectly --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, she's talking about, on the one hand, in the statement check-points --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I don't want to discuss the content at this moment of this in the presence of the witness. That is not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine with me. I just don't want to confuse the witness by misrepresenting what is in the statement, and I'm afraid we'll go down that road if we don't actually put to her what she actually said.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I put to her what she actually said, Your Honour. I read it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In page 23, Ms. Gustafson read out exactly what the witness said in her statement. Ms. Gustafson, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, do you have my question --

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. Am I allowed to look at my statements to read what I stated there?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Does the witnesses have the statements that she was given yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could the hard copies be given to Ms. Botteri.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have them with me. If you allow me, I can take them out of my purse.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The answer is - I'm not sure what page in the B/C/S -- about halfway down, the answer to question 16 of your most recent statement that you gave to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The one you gave to the Defence a few days ago.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 16?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry. Paragraph 16.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I see, paragraph 16. There -- there is no page 16.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the part I read out to you is about halfway down that answer.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: There's a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Question 16.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: There's a question numbered 16.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Perhaps the usher to assist the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: There's a question 16 and then there's an answer in the following paragraph. It should be a statement dated 2008.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it. In the statement dated so and so, is that what you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes. It's the answer to that question, beginning approximately halfway down, where it says: "In practice, the Split Military District commander could have issued orders," and following.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All right. I've read this portion. Could you now please put your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The question was: For a military police task, such as setting up a check-point, would a -- would an order from General Gotovina be a relevant order? For example, an order from General Gotovina to the military police to set up a check-point in a particular location, would that be a relevant order?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, no. I think this was within the competence of their basic tasks, but this is only my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Are you saying that you think setting up a check-point was within the competence of the basic tasks of the military police?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I mean, you stated earlier that General Gotovina's authority to -- over the military police was authority over their regular military police tasks, according to Article 9 of the rules. Would setting up a check-point be part of the regular military police tasks, pursuant to Article 9 of the rules?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not my area of expertise. I was not sufficiently acquainted with the work and rules of the military police. I just had general knowledge, and probably my statements says they are the result of that situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So, I mean, is it fair that you had no knowledge of the practical situation, in terms of whether General Gotovina issued orders to the military police to take steps, such as setting up check-point, patrolling, or detaining members of the HV who were found to be committing crimes? Is that correct you had no practical knowledge of the situation?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave my statements only in respect of the work that I did. So when I discussed the authority of the military police, what I was saying referred to those areas that had to do with military disciplinary liability, criminal responsibility, within the scope of my work, in the sense that it related to my work. But as for this portion, when I gave my statements, it did not refer to this type of activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So outside the scope of your particular role over disciplinary matters, would it be correct to say that you don't know what orders General Gotovina could issue over the military police?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander could issue, to the military police, I will reiterate, the commander, in keeping with the provisions of the rules on the conduct of the military police, on the work of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And earlier, in answer to one of my earlier questions about the HV members occupying flats illegally and General Gotovina's order to the military police to file criminal charges against the perpetrators who didn't move out, you agreed with me that his authority to do that stemmed from Article 9. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And just in relation to this, to your practical knowledge, in your 2007 statement, at paragraph 24, you said that you only took part in meetings of the Split Military District command and you presumed that General Gotovina held their meetings, and you thought that the 72nd Military Police commander would have attended such meetings. I don't think - I mean, unless you need to - I don't think -- my question isn't based on what you said in your statement. My question is: Did you attend any meetings between General Gotovina and Colonel Budimir?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, since the first part of the question refers to paragraph 24 --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: She's reading the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: My question was: Did you attend any meetings between General Gotovina and Colonel Budimir?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And do you recall being -- ever being present when General Gotovina gave Colonel Budimir any orders?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm moving to another topic. Perhaps it would be a good time to have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break and resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Botteri, I'd like to ask you a few questions about units that were temporarily subordinated to the Split Military District and the disciplinary procedures for such units, and you've discussed this matter in your various statements. In your Defence statement, you said: "The Split Military District could not have conducted disciplinary proceedings against members of the attached subordinate units; that is, it could have conducted them in extraordinary cases but the system was not set up to suit these cases. In fact, the reporting system was set up in such a manner that this could not happen." My question is: What was it about the reporting system that caused you to conclude that the Split Military District could not have conducted disciplinary proceedings against temporarily subordinated units, except in extraordinary cases?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that I stated that, and I stated that based on the provisions of the rules governing disciplinary matters. This statement that I made is completely true and based on the Code of Military Discipline, and based on the enactment which stipulated precisely the coverage of military districts and the fundamental principle derived from all the provisions of the Code of Military Discipline; namely, that it was not possible for any commander within the Military District of Split to conduct disciplinary proceedings against any member of another resubordinated unit or attached unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Which provision or provisions of the Code are you referring to specifically?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Code of Military Discipline, regardless of the fact that it governed offences that were, at first blush, minor, was rather complex, in fact, and complicated, I would say, in a formally legal sense. That meant that if you had to take legal action against an offender for a disciplinary offence or a disciplinary violation, you had to proceed, first of all, from the status of the offender, from his position; that is, his rank. You had to know whether he was an active duty military person --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I asked you to indicate which provision or provisions of the Code prevented commanders from disciplining temporarily subordinated units. Can you point to any particular provisions of the Code; or is your answer that it's just based on the Code as a whole?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am talking about the Code as a whole, and the powers were also stipulated by the legal document that stipulated the existence of several Military Districts.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you would agree that in Article 19 of the Code, it states that superior officers shall decide the disciplinary responsibility of their subordinates? Would you agree that one of the principles of military discipline is to provide a system where superiors can discipline their subordinates?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I have a copy of the Code, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. I have read Article 19.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And would you agree that one of the principles of a military disciplinary system is to provide a mechanism for superiors to discipline their subordinates?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, in principle, that there is a possibility for superior commanders to establish the disciplinary responsibility of their subordinates and pronounce disciplinary measures. However, I maintain that, in view of the complexity of the Code of Military Discipline, in practice, generally speaking, it was impossible to implement. Besides, Article 19 is general language. It says "superior commanders, superior officers." However, the Code of Military Discipline is something we cannot view in isolation from other documents that stipulated the powers of a specific commander. One of those legal documents was the division into several military districts. Therefore, Article 19, when it speaks of a superior officer, it means a superior officer in a particular military entity in which that superior officer is located. The system was not adapted to allow for the possibility to pronounce military disciplinary measures against a member of another attached or temporarily subordinated unit. In order to prosecute in the disciplinary sense any offender, you had to be aware of his status, whether he was an active military man, whether he had been mobilised as a conscript, what his rank was; and as soon you were in a position to request information about that, it was more practical not to go through with it at all. It was impossible to implement in practice.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, if General Gotovina wanted to discipline the commander of the 7th Guards Brigade who was subordinated to him, what is it about his awareness of his status, whether he was an active military man, whether he had been mobilised as a conscript, how are those obstacles to General Gotovina's ability to discipline the commander of the 7th Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object because it was asked and answered in the last answer, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I disagree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would join Ms. Gustafson in disagreeing with that proposition. Could you please answer the question, Ms. Botteri.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: My question was: How was General Gotovina's awareness of the status, whether he was an active military man, whether he had been mobilised as a conscript, how were those obstacles to General Gotovina's ability to discipline the commander of the 7th Guards Brigade who was subordinated to him?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I can't agree with the term "subordinated to him." What do you mean by saying "subordinated to him"?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I mean subordinated to him in the sense that General Gotovina was the superior of the 7th Guards Brigade commander who was his subordinate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Object to the formulation, Your Honour, and I'd ask for foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, you put it as a fact that --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it is in the Defence statement. I'm just looking for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The last sentence of answer -- the answer to question 19: "Another thing which draws attention is the fact that the report," she's talking about a statistical report of disciplinary measures, "didn't include units subordinated to the Split Military District which were not organic parts - e.g., the 7th Guards Brigade, 1st Croatian Guards Corps, or the 144th Guards Brigade, 2nd Battalion of the 9th Guards Brigade and the 81st Guards Battalion."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think the foundation is there. That's what the witness apparently said in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. My foundational question, though, goes to exactly to this answer. There is a little more subtlety than was put to her in that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but can you deal with that in cross-examination if you want to. It clearly states that it -- that the units mentioned were subordinated. That's what the text tells us. Now, Ms. Botteri, you said: "What do you mean by 'subordinated'?" I think that Ms. Gustafson meant exactly the same as what you said in your answer to question 19 in the statement you gave to the Defence. So, again, the question is to what extent would lack of knowledge on these background information, like when mobilised, et cetera, et cetera, whether that would be an obstacle for General Gotovina to exercise disciplinary powers against the commander of the 7th Guards Brigade, which, as you said, was subordinated to the military district -- Split Military District.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I say with full responsibility that from all my knowledge of the military system of the Croatian army, the 7th Guards Brigade was not subordinated to the commander of the Split Military District. The statements I have made -- first, in the 2004 statement, there was a mistake in translation and I corrected it in the 2007 statement, because I emphasise when I made my statements, I had problems with interpretation and the wrong understanding of the terms I was using on the part of the interpreter, which is quite understandable because legal systems differ. The statement that I gave to the Defence team, where I mentioned the 7th Guards Brigade, was a statement I gave precisely because I wanted to stress that I had problems related to the Prosecutor's misunderstanding of what I said about various military districts, and the fact that what I said did not mean at all that the 7th Guards Brigade was subordinated to the commander of the Split Military District.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your statement in 2008 says that it was subordinated, although not an organic part of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. Let me find that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the end of your answer to question 19, you there explained what was not included in your report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regardless of the fact that here we see language, the report does not include units that were subordinated to the Split Military District, it is it certain that at that moment I did not say it based on any knowledge that they would have been subordinated. Perhaps, when I was giving this statement, the train of my thoughts was directed, rather, at saying that looking at the overall operation, the 7th Guards Brigade was supposed, in its own reports, to include information about disciplinary measures pronounced and possible disciplinary infractions or violations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I have to understand your answer that if there's a temporary subordination of a not organic part of a military district, that the disciplinary powers rest with the other military district, rather than with the military district in which it, the brigade, operates? Is that how I have to understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You think so, or what's the basis of this thought?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm really sorry, Your Honour, but could you please repeat your question, once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's try to keep matters simple; and if I make a mistake, please correct me. I have a brigade, the 7th Guards Brigade. I temporarily put that brigade in the command structure of the Split Military District. That means, operationally, it becomes part of that military district. Now, with whom rests the disciplinary powers? With the command of the Split Military District or with the command of the military district this brigade would be part of, if it would not have been -- which is an organic part, if it would not have been moved to the operations of the Split Military District? Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really regret rising, but there is one thing I may wish to clarify with you in terms of the question without her being able to listen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the witness understands some English, I have to ask her to leave the courtroom for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's okay, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise, Ms. Botteri, but Mr. Misetic wants to raise an issue which it would not be appropriate for you to already hear about at this stage. Could you please follow Madam Usher for a second and remain standing by to return into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just so you understand, to know what my understanding is, perhaps we could use an example other than the 7th Guards Brigade. The 7th Guards Brigade didn't formally -- or wasn't a part of any military district. It was subordinated to directly to the Main Staff and then resubordinated as needed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will apologise, but I don't have these details all immediately on my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Given how specific the witness is in her answers, I wanted you to be aware that that may be an issue with her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that. Do you have a better example, because the 7th Guards Brigade, as such, is not vital for the information I'm seeking. Ms. Gustafson, do you have any problem? You may have a specific interest in mentioning the 7th Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, not specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I consult with my client for a second?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I should have formulated it in the negative, not being an organic part of, rather than the other way. I can even do without an example, Mr. Misetic, if you have a better suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm using the ones that are in her statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The 2nd Battalion, 9th Guards Brigade is organically part of the Gospic Military District. I'm also advised that there may be an issue with posing a question as to taking a disciplinary publish specifically against the a commander of a guards brigade. That's also something that lies in the, from our position, exclusive jurisdiction of the chief of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that should be an appropriate topic to raise in cross-examination. I don't think it should be a bar to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But you are put on notice that that apparently seems to be a specific issue. Could the witness be brought into the courtroom again. I apologise for perhaps not always following the strict adversarial procedures, but this Chamber takes the position that we'd like to understand what we hear and, therefore, seek clarification now and then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, you have mentioned in the last part of your answer to question 19 a number of units, among them the 2nd Battalion of the 9th Guards Brigade; and you said: "They were not organic parts of the Split Military District." You also said that they were subordinated. Could you tell us, with whom did the competence, the power rest to discipline -- to take disciplinary actions against members of the 2nd Battalion of the 9th Guards Brigade? Was it the command of the Split Military District, or was it any other authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly not the command of the Split Military District.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, if not the command of the Split Military District, could you tell us who then was competent to take disciplinary actions against members of that battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The battalion which was attached or belonged to the 7th Guards Brigade, so the command of the 7th Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it reads in your statement the 9th Guards Brigade. Did you misspeak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. The 7th Guards Brigade, yes. It was a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... do I understand that this battalion was at least under the, even if temporary, operational command of the Split Military District?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was the assistant commander for legal affairs. I can speak about the facts that I knew of, because they were within my competence. As for operational commands, I cannot speak about that, nor did I know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you said in your statement that they were subordinated to the Split Military District. If it was not an operational, even temporary, subordination, what was it then? I mean, what else is there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What it means is that even if they were operationally subordinated to the Split Military District Command, when it comes to military discipline, the applicable principle was the organic -- the organic element or the organic entity to which perpetrators belong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you give us the legal basis for this legal opinion; case law, legislation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A moment ago, in reply to a question, I mentioned a legal document. I can't recall what the name of this document was, but it dealt with the division of the area into various military districts. This is one of the documents upon which the competence relied in disciplinary matters, in matters of military discipline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you say you mentioned a legal document, you don't remember the name, but that's the document where we find it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not an expert in this field at all. If you referred to a legal document saying that we find the answer there, of course, this Chamber would very much like to have a look at that document. Could you assist us in identifying what it was? I don't remember whether you gave the name and you have forgotten about it, or whether you gave the name at all. I don't remember that you gave a name of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not mention the title of this document. In my reply, I also used the term that, as far as I could remember, I know of a legal document which discussed the matter of military districts. And in the same reply, I mentioned the Code of Military Discipline, which -- or, rather, from which it arose that in terms of military discipline, the commander of the military district is in charge of such perpetrators, the commander on whose territory of perpetrators are or happen to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you take to us where the territory is mentioned, or perhaps the parties could assist me. I remember that I think it was in Article 2 or 3 that commander of the military district was mentioned, but what seems to be the real issue is whether it's the organic command or the temporary operational command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm intend to deal with this at length in cross-examination. There's quite a bit of the material that has to be present the to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then perhaps I leave it to that. Again, I apologise. Perhaps we should wait for cross-examination sometimes to understand what the testimony is about. But if we would that always, we would miss quite a lot of understanding of what the evidence is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Agreed, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, we'll hear more about this at a later stage. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, just on the Code of Military Discipline, you agree that Article 26 of the Code allows a commander of a unit to issue disciplinary measures to offenders who are not members of their organic unit. And in your 2007 statement, you describe that provision as saying: "It was an exception to the rule in urgent cases the officer at hand may take disciplinary action against soldiers even if they are outside his unit." Article 26 states that: "Such orders may be issued if such measures are required for maintaining order and discipline." Would you agree that the system of military discipline allowed a commander to issue disciplinary measures against members of non-organic units, if the measures are required for maintaining order and discipline?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was an exception. I reiterate, however, that in practice, because of the overall system, as it was set up by the Code of Military Discipline, in practice, it was very infrequent and difficult to implement. In addition, we cannot overlook the fact that when reading in isolation a provision from a legal document, we have to view it in context of the overall document or the overall Code of Military Discipline in this particular case. A careful reading of Article 26 shows that the purpose, or, rather, the intent of the law-maker was for Article 26 to apply to some specific events, as may occur in actual life, because, as it is stated there, it says "commanders of units" -- or, rather, "of garrisons," and then in parentheses, it says "a base, a ship, barracks," and so on and so forth, "hospital," et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Court to read. This is it P1007. It's at page 9 of the English, and I'm not sure what page in B/C/S. I no longer have my copy but probably in page 3 or 4 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In fact, Ms. Botteri, it reads: "Commanders of units institutions, and garrisons (barracks, camps, medical institutions, ships, ports, et cetera) shall ..." --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's page 4 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Again, Ms. Botteri, the provision states that such measures may be implemented if they are required for maintaining order and discipline. Would you agree that that's what this provision provides for and that the system in military discipline provided for the same?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree; however, I have to note that this is an exception to the rule. This is applicable in exceptional circumstances. Also, we cannot overlook -- we cannot ignore paragraph 2 of this Article, which states the following: "In situation where an officer under paragraph 1 of this Article has decided that it is not necessary that an offender who does not belong to his unit be immediately punished, the matter shall be forwarded to the offender's superior officer to deal with." This means that paragraph 2, in a way, refers or stresses the need to regulate an exceptional situation for immediacy purposes, for urgent matters, and not to be implemented for general -- and not to provide for commanders in general to have the authority to implement disciplinary measures. So this is only to be used in exceptional situations. We have to know that barracks, camps, medical institutions, ships, ports, et cetera, are such entities where a member belonging to another organic entity can be only be temporarily stationed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Can he move now to 65 ter 3555.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, if you could look at this document, it's a document sent to your department, the legal affairs department of the Split Military District, on the 25th of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It states: "We are sending you the enclosed orders on disciplinary measures imposed by the Split Military District commander to the following members of the HV 2nd Infantry Battalion of the 9th Guards Brigade."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page of the English, it is signed by the commander of the 2nd Battalion of the 9th Guards Brigade, Ivica Arbanas. And if we could go to the next page in both documents, the orders are enclosed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You can see that this is an order issued on the 17th of May by General Gotovina to Tomislav Matkovic, member of the 9th Guards Brigade, 2nd Battalion. He is being disciplined for entering the area of disengagement on the 17th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page in the B/C/S, you can see that it is signed by General Gotovina. And if we scroll through the B/C/S, there are two identical orders for different members. In the English, there are no translations for these orders because they're the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you will see, Ms. Botteri, scrolling through, that two other members of the 2nd Battalion of the 9th Guards Brigade are being disciplined by General Gotovina for the same infraction.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please tell me whether I can see these orders in these materials. Are they in there?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No. You have to just look on the screen, they're not in the binders; although, I have a hard copy if that would assist you.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, if you don't mind, because it is easier when I have it right in front of me, when I have the complete documentary, rather than just seeing them in isolation, one from the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the document I gave to the witness include this 65 ter number and also 65 ter 3556; and, perhaps, we could go to that document now. The last document is a document from General Gotovina to the Main Staff, submitting these orders for evaluation.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, once you have had a look at these documents, if you could explain to the Court what your view is on the legal basis for imposing these measures. Have you had a chance to look at the documents, Ms. Botteri?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Do you notice that these orders invoke Articles 22 and 33 of the Code of Military Discipline. Article 22 states that the commander of a brigade or corps or more senior commanders shall be empowered to pronounce all disciplinary measures prescribed under these Code. These officers shall decide the responsibility of soldiers, guardsmen, reserve soldiers, and cadets for the offences specified in paragraph 1, Article 12.
