Article 33 of the Code refers to the required contents of a disciplinary order. These particular disciplinary orders don't refer to Article 26. Can I ask you again to explain to the Court your understanding of the legal basis for these orders. Do you have an understanding --

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The legal basis is Article 22, which is invoked in the preamble to this order; Article 22.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm finished with these document, Your Honour. I don't have if you have any follow-up questions, but I'd like it tender them, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objection. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 3555 becomes Exhibit number P1014; and 65 ter number 3556 becomes Exhibit number P1015.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1014 and P1015 are admitted into evidence. Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could move now to 65 ter 525, and if we could go to the next page on the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, I think you'll recognise this. It was described in two of your statements. It's a document from the 10th of November, 1995, authored by you, and it's a report on the third quarter statistics of disciplinary measures in the Split Military District. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And could we move to page 8 in the English and page six in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: These are the statistics for the quarter. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down to the bottom and blow up the letters underneath the chart, A through H, and if we could have the English of that as well. It should be on page 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, those letters, A through H, do those correspond to the disciplinary breaches listed in the Code of Military Discipline in Article 3, numbers 1 through 8? So, for example, Article 3, 7, commission of a crime for which proceedings are initiated ex officio, corresponds to letter G, and so on.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you've explained in your statement to the Defence that the military district received only those decisions on the implementation of disciplinary offences issued by brigade commanders and commanders of independent battalions. All other issued members were presented in the quarterly reports only as statistical data. My question is: The quarterly reports that you received from the unit, did they -- were they in the same form as this document, in other words, listing the number of disciplinary measures imposed under each provision of Article 3?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go back to the full page in the B/C/S and maybe show more of the page. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The report you received from the units, were they in the same form, indicating the number of measures imposed under each provision of Article 3?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm really sorry, Madam Prosecutor. My statement was misinterpreted when I said that we received reports only from the directly subordinated command. We received disciplinary measures for purposes of evaluation of irregularity from directly subordinated command. Statistical reports are something entirely different. We received statistical reports from directly subordinated commands, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, I am asking about --

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I understand that. I'm asking you what the form of those statistical reports that you received were in. Were they in the same form as this report that you compiled, in other words, listing the number of the disciplinary measures imposed under each provision of Article 3, indicating whether they were imposed on soldiers, guardsmen, or officers, and indicating the type of the punishment imposed?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Perhaps we can split to the English to show that column.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember clearly the form itself, whether it was the same form as the one used for subordinated units. I don't think it was the same. But their reports did contain numbers broken down by types and sanctions, and they also included information about the status of the offender, similarly as this one report made at command level.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. So these -- in these quarterly reports received from the units, did you have any indication in those reports of the type of conduct that was being disciplined, other than which provision of Article 3 was being invoked?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer this question with certainty because -- because the type of infraction was distinguished from the Code, decoded by the key that you had shown us and zoomed in on a moment ago. I don't remember the codes used by various units.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm just asking if there was any additional information on what type of conduct was being disciplined, other than breaking it down according to the provision of Article 3 of the Code.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what sense do you mean "additional information"?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: For example, a description of what the individual incidents were. Did the reports from the units actually describe in words what the incidents were, or was just these numbers.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. These were just ordinary statistical data, simple figures.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, so, if we look at the entry for the post code 8311 which is near the bottom, four from the bottom, further up. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: 8311 is the 6th Home Guard Regiment indicating 144 measures imposed for the quarter. And in the documents you were shown yesterday of the 83 incidents for August and September that were sent to the Split Military District, one of those dealt with a member of the 6th Home Guard Regiment. My question is: Based on the reporting system you've described, when you were compiling this report, would you have had any idea of what type of misconduct being punished for these 144 incidents, other than which provision of Article 3 they fell under?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, no? Just responding to your body language, but let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Perhaps if I could just get a reference to the document yesterday that counsel is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry. It was the documents underlying the chart that was 65 ter 6017, which actually reminds you me, Your Honour, I neglect neglected to get a number for that chart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No number was assigned to neither of the charts?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The second one was, was Your Honour. It was the first one that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it was the first one, the first one being the "known examples of." That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I have no objection to it being added to the 65 ter list and admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Ms. Gustafson, you're seeking leave to add it to the 65 ter list and have it admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 6017 becomes exhibit number P1016.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Did you understand my question, Ms. Botteri --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I could first give a decision --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would still like it repeated. We don't have the whole table shown on the screen. You mentioned the number 144, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that is the column showing the total, and I think we have to move down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In total, yes. Then further down, it's not 144. It's lower. You have to go lower for the total figure. That's 1.431. Is that the number you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No. I mean the number 144 for the entry for post code 8311, the 6th Home Guards Brigade, which is four from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good. Because I don't remember these codes for various units. So 8311 and the column where you see 144?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's right. My question is -- our records show that a report came to the Split Military District Command regarding one disciplinary measure, an individual measure taken against a member of the 6th Home Guard Regiment, and my question is: Based on the reporting system, when you compiled this report, did you have any idea what type of conduct was being disciplined for these 144 incidents, other than the break down for each provision of Article 3 that was being invoked?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just based on the code and the number, I have no other knowledge, no other information, such as a description. There's just the code and the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you move on Ms. Gustafson, the 65 ter 6017 is admitted into evidence, and this implies that leave is granted to add it to your 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you a couple of questions about reserve units. In your 2007 statement, you said: "The rules of the military discipline and the possibilities of taking disciplinary action were not applied equally toward reserve forces as they were towards professional units." Then, in your Defence statement in paragraph 10, you said: "It was my subjective view that the commanders would rather get rid of their problematic reservist by simply substituting them for another soldier in cooperation with the defence office than to engage in conducting proceedings to establish disciplinary responsibility." In light of this practice that you've described, my question is: Was there any concern amongst the Split Military District Command that reserve soldiers might not have been properly or adequately punished for their misconduct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask, then, that the rest of the sentence be read to her in light of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, I invite you to meet the request of Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I can. I'm not sure it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The rest of the sentence says: "For many, this presented a graver punishment than the one prescribed by the Code." My question is: Was there any concern amongst the Split Military District Command that reserve soldiers might not have been properly or adequately punished for their misconduct.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Which paragraph is that in my statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, the question is a simple one. Was there any concern amongst the Split Military District Command that reserve soldiers might not have be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, the question may have been simple. If you put a certain portion of a statement to a witness, and if she has apparently difficulties in fully remembering what is in there, she should have an opportunity it re-read it, even if the question is perfectly clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Perhaps the usher could assist the witness in finding the answer to question 10 in her 2008 statement. It's on page 5. Sorry. That was in the English. Sorry. It's the answer to question 10.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. [Interpretation] All legal regulations, including the regulations on military discipline, applied equally to active duty personnel and reserve personnel of the Croatian army; however, in practice, in view of the variety of disciplinary measures and sanctions, many of them were ineffectual when applied to the reserve personnel of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Article 10 of the Code provides for caution, reprimand, confinement to barracks for up to seven days, and detention in military custody for up to 30 days; and we've also seen measures deducting the pay, particularly from guardsmen. Now, whether or not a reserve soldier was being paid or not, or how much, would you agree that a caution, a reprimand, a confinement to the barracks, or detention in military custody were all measures that could be applied to reserve soldiers?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's what I just said, that the Code of Military Discipline applied equally to both active duty and reserve soldiers. But I said that in my statement that it was my subjective perception that many commanders of reserve soldiers got rid of them by simply demobilizing them. If you allow me to explain, the main task of every military commander, the primary task of military commander, is to ensure order and discipline in his unit, in order to perform his mission. If a reserve soldier is creating problems, then - this is my personal opinion - the commander was tempted to get rid of that soldier by demobilizing him, rather than starting a very complicated and long process that would lead to the punishment of such a soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, my objection is in light of the question. For partial readings of provisions of Code, I think the witness should be entitled to see the complete Article which she is being referred to so that she can provide an answer. Because if she had the Code in front of her, she might be able to respond.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: She has the Code.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: She has the Code in front of her; and, of course, at the same time, we should not forget that this witness apparently has worked in this area of law for quite a period of time, but we could ask her. Ms. Botteri, if you feel any need to further read legal provisions in legal instruments that are presented to you, please let me know. You can ask for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just add, I don't have a -- I agree with that proposition. My specific objection, though, is if portions of it are going to be read to her, then she should be entitled to see the entire provision. It Article 11, and then it would make --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would always, Ms. Gustafson, mention the portion you're reading, I don't remember whether you did it in this case, so that the witness has an opportunity to look at the text.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I did, and I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the witness has had a lot of time now, I think, to read what she apparently is reading.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: She --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: She answered that question, so I would just like to move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd just ask, Ms. Botteri, is it your view, then, that the practice of simply demobilizing a problematic reserve soldier was sufficient disciplinary punishment that was, in your view, adequate?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to clarify also on your previous question. I feel the need to say that it's not true that reserve soldiers were not subject to sanctions envisage the by the Code of Military Discipline. But along with the punishments prescribed by the Code, there were also, in application, some sanctions that were not prescribed in legal texts that were applied; and such unprescribed punishments were harder on the soldier concerned, much harder than any sanction actually envisaged by the Code, and we can see that from the Code itself. For disciplinary infractions, under Article 10, there was the possibility of caution, reprimand, detention in a military detention facility up to 30 days. That applied only to soldiers, not NCOs and officers. Also, another possibility was the suspension of leave and prohibition of exit from the barracks. I apologise to the interpreters. I have just been told that I'm reading too fast.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And when you talk about unprescribed punishments, is --

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: When you talk about unprescribed punishments, is this the demobilization practice that you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, I'd ask that she be allowed to finish the last portion of her answer concerning Article 11.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask that she direct her answers to my questions more precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's in Article 11. That is what I was hoping she was going to get to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness, when you started requesting a question, the witness spoke as well, Ms. Gustafson. Perhaps you should allow --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 11 speaks of disciplinary infractions, and it enumerates the various sanctions that may be pronounced for these infractions; namely, those that apply only to officers and NCOs, and those were suspension of promotions for one to two years --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there, Ms. Botteri. Ms. Gustafson's questions are focussing on the, well, let's say, informal sanctions which were not provided for by the law. So, perhaps, mentioning everything that is in the law might not be a focussed answer to what she apparently wants to ask you. Ms. Gustafson, perhaps you could phrase or rephrase the question you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Enumerating these sanctions envisaged under Article 11, I only wanted to explain why I had this feeling, this subjective perception, that unprescribed punishments, such as demobilization, were much harder and more drastic a punishment for such a soldier, especially --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- if we bear in mind the social circumstances --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, it's clear that it's your assessment that these sanctions provided for by law were perhaps often of a less serious impact on the perpetrator. Ms. Gustafson, your next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And were these informal measures, like the practice of demobilizing problematic reserve soldiers, was there any systematic reporting of those measures to the Split Military District Command?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Demobilization was carried out through the competent defence office, not through the command of the military district. It was between the brigade commander and the competent defence office. If there had been reports about that, then it would no longer be my subjective perception or a feeling. We would have documentation about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry. I wasn't finished with 65 ter 525, if that could be brought back up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, if this will be of the first of a series of questions, I think we first should have a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask one more question on this, and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And conclude your examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have more questions that I'd like to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's see. If you put this question, then we will discuss about timing.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we can go back to the chart on, I think, the last page in B/C/S, page 6 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Botteri, you see the first post code is 1080. That's the Split Military District Command. My question for you is: If General Gotovina had taken any disciplinary measures against any of his subordinates in the third quarter, would those measures have been recorded here under the first -- in the first row of this chart?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could I have a number for this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number P1017.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked for a number because I saw no signs of objections. P1017 is admitted into evidence. Ms. Gustafson, we'll have a break, but we'll first ask the witness to follow Madam Usher to leave the courtroom. We'll have a break, Ms. Botteri, of approximately 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, how much more time you would need?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If I could have another 15 minutes, Your Honour, I think I could cover the basics of what else I wanted to cover.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Usually, if the Chamber says that we'll see how the testimony develops, that is a kind of, well, a warning is perhaps too strong, but at least a reminder that time should be used in an efficient way. Here, we have observed how the testimony developed, and we'll grant you the time you need.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's fine with me. I just wanted t make the Court aware that I am going to need a substantial of amount on cross. In light of the fact that tomorrow is a Friday, and I know the Court's preference to let witnesses leave on a Friday, I wanted to the Court to be aware of it right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that. I don't know how much time you had in mind, Mr. Misetic. Perhaps we could already inquire into that, but also tell me whether you calculated the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I understand your point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I would say, the not fully 100 percent focussed responsiveness of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Much like Ms. Gustafson, my two and a half may be somewhere around twice that, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask other Defence counsel. Mr. Kay, let's say with your initial assessments, and then the Chamber will be able to see how also in cross-examination the testimony develops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, for my part, it depends what remains to be asked by the Prosecution, what goes before me, but I have in mind a half an hour slot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour, it depends on the previous examination; but as from now on, I wouldn't have any questions on that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No questions. So there is a good expectation that we could finish the testimony of this witness by tomorrow, but it still is full of uncertainty, to say the least. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, you may proceed. But, first, Ms. Botteri, I would like to invite you to focus your answers very much on the question. If any further details are expected from you, the person examining you will certainly ask for these details. So would you please focus your answers on the core of the question that has been put to you. Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, I'd like to turn to another topic now which is the 5th of August, 1995, and your trip to Knin on that date. And in your first statement, you explained that when you heard that Knin had been liberated, you decided to go to Knin to be with your command. "We left Split at about 11.00 on the 5th of August, arriving at about 1600 hours at Knin castle, where all the political representatives had gathered." My first question is: Which other members of the Split Military District Command went to Knin on the 5th August?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question. I don't know how.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You said you went to Knin on the 5th of August because you wanted to be with your command. Who else from the command was in Knin on the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I went to Knin; although I didn't have to go, I decided to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, could you please tell us who were there, not whether you went there voluntarily, whether you had to go there. The question is quite simple: Who else of the Split Military District Command were there in Knin on that day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw some people from the 4th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And who from the command was there? You've named some of these people in your statement. Rahim Ademi, Gotovina's Chief of Staff, was he in Knin on the 5th of August? Yes, no, or I don't know.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And what about Coric, assistant commander for logistics?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see him either. I don't know if he was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: What about Ivan Zelic, assistant commander for information and political activities?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I didn't meet him either.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Do you remember anyone from the Split Military District Command being there.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You're shaking your head. Is that no?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: My driver was with me, a lawyer from my service.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm not interested in your driver or a lawyer from your service. The question was about members of the command. If you can't remember, could you please just say you can't remember and we can move on.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you said, in your statement, you arrived in Knin at about 1600 hours. My question is: Did you see any signs of combat in Knin at that time?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And what did you see?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Knin town, I stayed on the main road, main street. I saw many soldiers; and, at one point, I think I saw a soldier from the 4th Brigade being injured and then he was carried away. The street that I was on looked like a street through which an army had passed. There were a lot of broken windows on shop, shop windows.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Did you see -- were there any signs to you that the fighting was still going on; or did the fighting appear to you to be over?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were no signs of fighting going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you said you saw a lot of broke windows on shop, shop windows. Did you see -- did it appear to you that the items in the shop were still in the shop; or did it appear to you that items had been taken out of the shops on which the windows were broken?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, halfway, sort of; some were gone.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So, just to clarify, in some of the shops where the windows were broken, you saw that items were gone?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to turn to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I ask one clarifying question. You told us about a soldier from the 4th Brigade being injured. Did you see him getting this injury and could you tell us what you saw; or is it that you saw a soldier of the 4th Brigade who had been injured and was carried away? Did you see the moment of being injured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I saw when the medical service came to assist him, and I think it was the fatal outcome, based on what I learned later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If the witness could be shown Exhibit D32.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, do you recognise this document as the service regulations of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Were these regulations in effect in 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we turn to page 18 in the B/C/S and page 21 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, if could you read Article 52, which states: "The garrison commander is responsible for billeting, order, discipline, and service in the garrison. All units and institutions within the garrison are subordinate to the garrison commander, as regards the issues of order, discipline, and service." My question for you is: Did garrison commanders have disciplinary authority and could garrison commanders take disciplinary measures against members of units and institutions within the garrison?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Should we establish, first of all, a foundation of the knowledge by this witness of such a matter? I know it's a matter of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- some expertise, and let's find out if that's the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I allow Ms. Gustafson to put this question without any prior exercise in relation, in respect of this witness. Ms. Gustafson, perhaps you repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The question, Ms. Botteri, was: Could garrison commanders take disciplinary measures against members of units and institutions within the garrison.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer your question. I think that I said in my first statement given to the Office of the Prosecutor that the status and powers or authority within the garrison were not a matter that was clear to me, and there's nothing I can say about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Botteri.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Gustafson. Ms. Botteri, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Misetic. Mr. Misetic is counsel for Mr. Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Botteri.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You were asked some questions this morning about a commission that had been established to determine who had unlawfully entered into some participants in Split, and it was represented to you that this was an example of a commission being formed to investigate, at least in part, disciplinary infractions against "unknown offenders." And I would like to show you the actual order that General Cervenko, the Chief of Staff, sent to the Split Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So if I may please have 1D58-0032, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this is the actual order that General Cervenko issued to General Gotovina on the 23rd of August in which General Gotovina is being ordered to form this commission on the basis of information that has been given to General Cervenko. And if you look through that, General Cervenko actually orders that you, as the assistant commander for legal affairs, be a part of that commission, and General Cervenko seemed to order who else would be parts of that commission. It orders that -- that the disciplinary responsibility be established. Section V states: "That the commander of the Split MD is obligated to immediately initiate disciplinary proceedings." And towards the end, at the bottom, when it talks about the military police, it says: "... and file criminal charges in cooperation with the military," it should say military police not military post office," to the competent military prosecutor's office in Split." So General Cervenko did not, first of all, as you see in the order, he did not cite Article 9 of the military police regulations and suggest that General Gotovina had this power on his own. General Cervenko says, "In cooperation with the military police ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which number?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm still listening on channel, Your Honour, so I will be cautious of the speed of my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In section V of the order, in the Croatian version, if you would read the last three lines of section V, it says: "In cooperation with the military police..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In cooperation with the military police, file criminal charges to the competent military prosecutor's office in Split." Right. I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Cervenko did not say to General Gotovina, "Use your powers to order the military police to conduct a criminal investigation." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... turn to the next page in the Croatian, please, and in the English as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, attached to the order is a letter from the owners of the apartment building to General Cervenko --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... by the name, the persons who are members, according to this letter, of the 4th Guards Brigade, by name, who had unlawfully entered these apartments. Do you see that? Do you recall that as part of your work on the commission?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So, let's explain this now. The disciplinary investigation began with specific names of specific perpetrators. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, in any disciplinary --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please speak into the microphone to his right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're invited to speak into the microphone at your right, which --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Right. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: With respect to disciplinary proceedings for major violations of discipline, even if the commander had eye-witnesses who told him about this major violation, he would still have to, under the rules, begin a process of affirming that individual's disciplinary responsibility before the military disciplinary court. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting. I just -- Mr. Misetic stated that the letter identified by name the persons who are members, according to the letter, of the 4th Guards Brigade, and maybe it's on a different page. I don't see those names on this page, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] if we can turn the page in the Croatian version, and the English, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So my question, or my point - and you tell me if you think I'm wrong - but any disciplinary proceeding starts off only with a suspicion that the person breached military discipline until that person's responsibility is formally affirmed in front of the relevant authority under the Code that is responsible for confirming that person's responsibility. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... ask that this exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D879.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D879 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Registrar, if we could now have P1013, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you a preliminary question, Ms. Botteri. As the assistant in the military district command, it's true, is it not, that, oftentimes, you would write up an order for General Gotovina's signature? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could go to the last page in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And was it common practice in the Split Military District Command that people who were in charge of different areas would oftentimes right up the order that needed to be issued and General Gotovina would review it and sign it?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go -- yes, that's the right -- sorry. If we could go to the prior page in the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And were you aware that sometimes people were authorised to sign documents on General Gotovina's behalf even, if it was necessary?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, you're looking at this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could, I believe, find the right page in the English, I believe it's the next page. It's dated 8 September.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this is the order you were asked about this morning, and it says -- as written, it says: "I hereby order," and then part 1 b talks about ordering the 72nd Military Police Battalion commander to file criminal charges. Now, are you aware of the practice or was it a routine practice when the Split Military District Command received an order from the Main Staff that it would often repeat the basic contents of that order to its subordinated units? Was that a common practice?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was common practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And this order says that it's based on the order of General Cervenko which I just showed you. However, unlike General Cervenko's order, which says to file the reports in cooperation with the military police, this order, as written, talks about ordering them to file. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In comparing the order of General Cervenko, which we just discussed, that it said that General Gotovina should act in cooperation with the military police. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The results of your commission here are now being reported back to General Cervenko, and the order says that, on its face, that it is being issued pursuant to General Cervenko's order. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. But General Cervenko's order, you agreed with me before, doesn't say to General Gotovina to order the military police to do anything. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So, is it possible that when this order was written and someone was perhaps following General Cervenko's order that the language used did not mirror the language that General Cervenko used?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you a general question. Outside of this order, have you ever seen in your years of work in the Split Military District or did the Prosecution ever show you any other order by General Gotovina to the military police to file criminal charges? Have you ever seen any other order like that, other than this?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, you were shown yesterday --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm switching topics, Your Honour. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see. The suggestion is that it was just passing an order of identified persons. I'm just trying to compare the list of names that were reported by the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's not my suggestion, Your Honour. I'm saying the commission was formed on the basis of specific --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the issue apparently was, is this a commission which deals with the identified perpetrators or unknown perpetrators? Now, I see that the commission is established. Perhaps we could move to the second page of what we see on the screen now as well. I see a letter which apparently starts some kind of a procedure, mentioning persons who have illegally occupied apartments. Now, in the follow-up, I see, if I'm not mistaken and, therefore, I would like to check that, I see orders to take measures against persons. The names of the persons have been identified of importance because they were apparently known suspects, not unknown suspects. I'm just comparing by number and by name these lists and see whether the one is and that is at least what I understood to be the suggestion is just a follow-up of what happened earlier. Now, I haven't got this. I have to play with my screens, rather than having hard copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could, Your Honour, tell you that by tomorrow morning I'll get you the answer to that, just so that I can fish what I have to do today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fine, fine. You know what my --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me also state --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- on my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- that the issue for us, as well, is you're talking about real property. Someone is either in the apartment or not in the apartment, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- it's a point of argument for later, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that point as well. I'm just wondering to what extent --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the language was copied from one to another and whether then also the names are copied from one order to another --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... whether it is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I will take care of that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will deal with that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- in the morning. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, you were asked about a chart that talked about actions taken by General Gotovina concerning disciplinary measures in August and September 1995. Now, let me ask you: How did these matters or why did these matters come to the attention of the Split Military District? Do you recall the chart?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In what sense do you mean how it was brought to the attention?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Exhibit P1010 on the screen, please -- or P1016. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, actually this is the second chart, but it is just as well. I have some questions for you on this as well. Why are these matters being reported to the Split Military District Command?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certain units reported to the Military District of Split because we had the job to provide the totality of this information to the administration for general affairs in the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... about General Gotovina assessing the imposed disciplinary measure. My question is: Can you tell the Court what -- in what instances would General Gotovina be required to assess a disciplinary measure?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Gotovina was in a position to assess the regularity and the adequacy of an individual disciplinary measure, only if that disciplinary measure had been pronounced by his direct subordinate. Looking at military hierarchy, it could only have been a disciplinary measure pronounced by the commander of the brigade or the independent battalion that had the status of brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... explain that if -- well, let's take the 4th Guards Brigade as an example. Let's say General Krsticevic, the commander of the 4th Guards Brigade, issues a disciplinary measure against his subordinate, would that -- would that be an instance where General Gotovina would review the disciplinary measure?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, did he review every disciplinary measure or only those measures that were appealed?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He evaluated the adequacy of all disciplinary measures pronounced by the brigade commander with the proviso that this evaluation of adequacy did not deal with the merits. It was an evaluation of procedural adequacy; that is, whether it was in keeping with the Code of Military Discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the order was submitted for evaluation, not the accompanying documentation. If an appeal was filed, then that appeal was decided.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So the only time that -- if there was an appeal, then that would be an instance where you receive the complete file and you would be able to reevaluate the merits. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Only in cases of appeal. Then, at our own request, we would get the documentation. Evaluation of regularity did not require the provision of a file. That is also in the Code.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, let's take the next level. If a battalion commander of the 4th Guards Brigade issues a disciplinary measure, who reviews that disciplinary measure?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a battalion commander issues a disciplinary measure, it is evaluated for irregular latter by the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... whose job it is to review the disciplinary measure imposed?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and it involves --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I often see in the transcript "[Previous translation continues] ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore, we should take breaks. Could you re-start with your question which now appears on line 3, page 79.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is where a question is put --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Battalion commander, is that it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see an answer on page 79, line 1: "If a battalion commander issues a disciplinary measure, it is evaluated for regularity by the brigade commander." Then you put a new question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, Your Honour. I'll finish up in two minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me repeat that question: The disciplinary publish issued by the battalion commander, that would be reviewed for its regularity by General Krsticevic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if the soldier wanted to appeal, the soldier who was issued the disciplinary measure by the battalion commander, wished to appeal, he would appeal to General Krsticevic as well. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And my last question for today: Is this the way that the system functioned all the way down the chain of command? In other words, the direct subordinate commander of the commander that issued the disciplinary measure would be the one who would review the measure?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... last question: At the level of -- from General Krsticevic, acting in his capacity as the person reviewing a disciplinary measure, from that level below, is it true that the Split Military District Command would not receive any information about disciplinary measures imposed, except in the form of the statistics that you talked about earlier this morning?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... done for today, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any matter remaining, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm told I may have misspoken, if I could just have one second. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I think it might be page 79, line 8. It should read: "In other words, the direct superior commander..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, and I thank counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Botteri, we'll adjourn for the day. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00. I again instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about the testimony, whether already given or still to be given. We adjourn until tomorrow, Friday, 31st of October, 9.00 in the morning, Courtroom I.
